# Control Plane Principles {.unnumbered}

Part I establishes the core operating system and control primitives of agentic runtimes. When inference ceases to be an isolated request and becomes an ongoing trajectory, the runtime must manage stateful descriptors, bound non-deterministic control topologies, and schedule heavy-tailed workloads across shared accelerator clusters.

::: {#pri-vol3-invariant-closure .callout-principle title="The Invariant Closure Principle"}

**Invariant**: Safety, resource budgets, and recovery invariants cannot be enforced at the single-token or single-request layer; the atomic unit of systems management must be the closed-loop trajectory.

**Implication**: An architecture that attempts to manage agents at the prompt layer without runtime encapsulation guarantees budget overruns and unbounded failure cascades.

:::

::: {#pri-vol3-stateful-descriptors .callout-principle title="Stateful Descriptor Binding"}

**Invariant**: The runtime must maintain an authoritative, kernel-managed descriptor (the Agent Control Block) governing identity, capabilities, memory pointers, and recovery vectors across time.

**Implication**: An agent's cognitive belief state cannot be snapshotted via bit-exact memcpy; descriptors must manage capabilities and resource leases rather than internal neural activations.

:::

::: {#pri-vol3-bounded-topologies .callout-principle title="Bounded Dynamic Execution"}

**Invariant**: Non-deterministic reasoning loops must be bounded by deterministic state machine topologies; execution loops require cycle detection and monotonic progress invariants.

**Implication**: Unconstrained peer-to-peer swarms create semantic livelocks; production architectures standardize on unidirectional supervisor-worker DAGs.

:::
